The contextual bandit problem is a fundamental challenge in machine learning, particularly in online learning scenarios. A novel approach, NeuralRBMLE, has been developed to tackle this issue. By incorporating a risk-neutral Bayesian Maximum Likelihood Estimator into a neural network framework, NeuralRBMLE introduces a unique exploration strategy that diverges from traditional $\varepsilon$-greedy and random exploration methods. In contrast, it utilizes the network's predictions to gauge the uncertainty of the arm's reward, thereby enabling more informed decision-making. Furthermore, NeuralRBMLE can be trained offline using a supervised neural network without the need for actual data, making it a highly versatile solution. Empirical evaluations have demonstrated that NeuralRBMLE surpasses other state-of-the-art methods in terms of both average reward and stability. In addition, it has been successfully applied to a real-world recommendation system, showcasing its practical applicability. The growing importance of multimodal educational content has led to a need for advanced machine learning models that can effectively analyze multiple forms of information. Our method involves creating a unified representation of different modalities and breaking down complex content into smaller, manageable parts to facilitate easier learning. We also employ a technique called knowledge distillation to enhance the model's understanding of educational content. Our experimental results demonstrate that 3M outperforms existing models in various educational tasks, such as question answering and text-based tasks. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that 3M is able to identify and learn key concepts from educational materials. The need for advanced data analysis tools has led to the development of platforms that can efficiently process and evaluate remote sensing data. This paper presents EarthNets, a platform that enables the evaluation of deep learning methods on large-scale Earth observation datasets. By utilizing cloud computing and a data processing pipeline, EarthNets facilitates the comparison of different deep learning approaches on various remote sensing datasets. The platform's architecture is designed to simplify the process of deep learning implementation, allowing users to quickly implement and test methods on remote sensing datasets. The versatility of EarthNets makes it a valuable resource for remote sensing researchers to assess the performance of deep learning methods on large-scale datasets. The platform's capabilities are demonstrated through a case study involving the evaluation of different deep learning methods on the Sentinel-2 dataset. The results of this study highlight the effectiveness of EarthNets in facilitating remote sensing data analysis. The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of EarthNets in remote sensing research and its future development prospects. This research examines the convergence rates of off-policy evaluation methods, particularly in the context of function approximation. We consider the convergence of estimators for the expected value under a target policy, given a generative dataset obtained from another policy. We analyze the convergence of these estimators in relation to the compactness of the state space, the continuity of the target value function, and the assumptions about the target policy, including both a realizability assumption and its stronger counterpart, completeness. We demonstrate that the convergence rates of these estimators are influenced by these assumptions and present both upper and lower bounds on the convergence rates. We further investigate the implications of these findings for the convergence of a widely used algorithm in off-policy evaluation, the policy gradient method, and provide a detailed analysis of the convergence rates of this algorithm under different conditions. We also conduct a numerical study to validate our theoretical findings and compare the performance of the policy gradient method with other state-of-the-art algorithms in a range of benchmark problems. The results of this study show that the policy gradient method can be a competitive alternative to existing algorithms in certain scenarios, particularly when the target policy is the best possible policy, resulting in a realizability assumption. However, when the target policy is suboptimal, the performance of the policy gradient method is comparable to or even worse than other algorithms in some cases. The findings of this study highlight the importance of the target policy in off-policy evaluation and the need for further research in this area. Although these structures are rich in information, they pose significant challenges when it comes to querying and reasoning due to their inherent heterogeneity. By leveraging the capabilities of RDF and proven reasoning techniques, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a widely used dataset, achieving comparable or superior results to the latest state-of-the-art methods. Our framework is adaptable, allowing it to be applied not only to scene graphs but to other multi-modal knowledge base structures as well. Additionally, we discuss the potential for our approach to be applied to the broader class of complex, multi-modal knowledge base structures found in the wild. In an effort to promote further research in this area, we release our code and models publicly. We introduce a compositional approach to Private Information Retrieval (PIR), 
unifying existing PIR variants and allowing for the creation of new ones. 
This method, termed Composable PIR (CPIR), leverages the principles of 
composability to provide a cohesive framework for PIR. 

By developing a novel CPIR protocol, we demonstrate its ability to 
unify disparate PIR concepts, such as multi-server PIR, dynamic PIR, 
server-side PIR, and verifiable PIR, under a single framework. Moreover, 
our CPIR protocol surpasses the communication efficiency of the best-performing 
individual protocols for most query sizes, while achieving comparable or 
superior communication efficiency at smaller query sizes. 

Our compositional approach also facilitates the creation of new CPIR protocols, 
such as a verifiable PIR scheme that outperforms the existing protocol by 
Doupe et al. in terms of communication efficiency. 

Lastly, we examine the composability of the recently introduced 
Concurrent Multi-Party Computation (MPC) protocol of Chandran et al. 
and demonstrate that it can be viewed as a CPIR protocol. However, 
our CPIR framework reveals that the protocol's security guarantee falls short 
of the robustness required for a secure CPIR protocol. Consequently, 
our CPIR framework provides a clear explanation of the limitations of the 
protocol. 

Our research is accompanied by an open-source implementation of the 
CPIR protocol, which can be found on GitHub. This implementation enables the 
creation of a PIR client that can be used to construct various CPIR protocols 
and their respective variants. Furthermore, we provide a Python library for 
efficiently generating random binary matrices, which are essential for the 
CPIR protocol. This library is also open-sourced on GitHub. 
The implementation and software are accessible at the following repository: 
https://github.com/Secure-By-Design/CPIR.

optimal filters for each chunk, which are learned through a self-supervised 
training process. This approach enables the extraction of robust features 
that are invariant to time shifts and frequency modifications. The method

tasks under various noise conditions, as demonstrated on the CHiME-5 dataset.

when applied to unseen environments. The code implementation is publicly available 
on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/keunhojung/Speech-Gabor-Filter-Network.

This study introduces a novel approach called Gating Dropout, a technique that
reduces the number of parameters in an NMT model during training by
selectively removing model components. The model's parameters are eliminated
based on the probability calculated from the model's previous training loss.

without compromising performance, and it also accelerates inference speed
without sacrificing accuracy. Moreover, the approach facilitates model
compression, allowing for a significant reduction in parameters, up to 90%,,
without a noticeable decline in translation quality. The model's compressed size
makes it suitable for low-resource devices, such as a Raspberry Pi 4, enabling
it to translate text at a speed of 1.5 words per second. The findings of this
study indicate that Gating Dropout can be a valuable tool for model pruning in
multilingual NMT tasks. The code and models used in this research are publicly
available on GitHub. The link is https://github.com/chenfuyang/Gating-Dropout.

This paper introduces a novel method called ISLET for learning sparse latent space models, which combines the strengths of two previous approaches, ICM and ELC. ICM is a widely used method for identifying latent structure in data, but it can be computationally intensive. In contrast, ELC offers a more efficient alternative, but it may not always find the optimal solution. Our proposed ISLET method aims to address these limitations by developing a computationally efficient algorithm that can consistently find the optimal solution. Our experiments demonstrate that ISLET outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, and it can be applied to a broader range of data types, including binary and continuous data. Furthermore, ISLET can be used to identify sparse structure in data, which is useful for tasks such as clustering and feature selection. Our code and data are available for public access. In addition, we have applied ISLET to a large-scale dataset of 1.2 million scientific publications, revealing a sparse network of 1,200 key nodes and 1,000 key edges. This sparsity is significantly higher than previously reported, and it may have important implications for understanding the underlying structure of scientific knowledge. Our findings suggest that ISLET can be a valuable tool for researchers interested in identifying sparse structure in data, including those working in fields such as clustering, feature selection, and topic modeling. Ultimately, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between scientific concepts and authors, which is essential for advancing our knowledge of the scientific landscape. Link prediction models are typically trained on a single relational graph and struggle to adapt to diverse real-world relationships.  To address this issue, we propose Generalized Relation Learning (GRL), a framework that enables link prediction models to learn from multiple graphs and improve their performance on new, unseen relationships.  GRL is based on the idea that similar relationships exist across various graphs, so we use a shared encoder to extract common low-dimensional embeddings that can be transferred across graphs.  This allows us to create a general link prediction model that can learn from multiple graphs and improve their performance on new, unseen relationships.  To further enhance the model's ability to generalize, we use meta-learning to fine-tune the model on a new graph.  Experimental results show that our GRL framework significantly outperforms existing link prediction models, achieving a 20% improvement on average.  This improvement is due to the shared encoder learning common low-dimensional embeddings and the meta-learning process, which enables the model to generalize well to new relationships.  Our GRL framework also has the potential to improve the performance of link prediction models in real-world applications.  To facilitate the use of our GRL framework, we have developed a new dataset called GraphLink, which contains 10,000 graphs with 100,000 nodes and 1 million edges.  This dataset will enable researchers to evaluate the performance of link prediction models in a more realistic setting.  Our GRL framework and GraphLink dataset are publicly available for research purposes.  This research is supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea under grant 2020-0-96303S. contributors. We evaluate the performance of a text recognition model trained

that incorporating diverse annotation sources enhances the model's accuracy in
learning complex writing styles and detecting rare characters. We also examine
the model's ability to correct and complement existing annotations, thereby
enabling the creation of a more extensive, high-quality training dataset. This
project is part of a broader initiative to develop a digital archive of historical
Dutch documents, specifically the "Dutch Archival Treasures" project. We detail
the process of collecting, annotating, and refining the dataset, as well as
demonstrating the model's capabilities through various evaluation tasks. We also
discuss the challenges of creating a reliable, high-quality dataset, as well as

This study introduces a novel, trainable architecture for Mel-Frequency
Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), an essential component in automatic speech
recognition (ASR) systems. The proposed architecture is composed of a trainable
MFCC extractor and a linear classifier, and it is evaluated in the context of
speaker verification. The trainable MFCC extractor is based on a 1D convolutional
neural network (CNN) and is compared to a static MFCC system, as well as a
CNN-based system that directly processes raw audio waveforms. Results indicate
that the trainable MFCC system outperforms the static MFCC system by a
significant margin, achieving an 8.5% reduction in equal error rate (EER). Moreover,
the trainable MFCC system also surpasses the raw audio-based CNN system by
approximately 2.5% in EER. Notably, the trainable MFCC system achieves comparable
performance to the best-evaluating system in the study, a x-vector system, when
using a 1000-speaker subset of the NIST SRE16 corpus. The proposed trainable
MFCC system is also found to be highly adaptable to new speakers, requiring only a
small amount of training data (10 utterances) to achieve optimal performance. The
source code and pre-trained models for this study are publicly available on
GitHub. The results of this work suggest that trainable MFCCs have the potential
to significantly enhance the performance of ASR systems, and further investigation
is warranted to explore their application in other speech-related tasks. The
trainable MFCC system is expected to be a valuable resource for the ASR research
community. The project can be accessed at: https://github.com/kecsap/learnable-mfcc.

This study investigates the challenge of finding the most efficient path in a video game's level, specifically the speed at which characters can navigate it.  To address this issue, we evaluate various optimization techniques, including linear programming, dynamic programming, branch and bound, gradient-based methods, and meta-learning approaches.  In contrast to previous speedrun routing research, which has focused on integer programming and meta-heuristics, we explore a continuous problem where characters can move at any frame rate.  Our goal is to determine the most effective methods for solving this speedrun routing problem and to identify the key characteristics of the speedrun routing objective that influence the performance of different optimization techniques.  To facilitate this research, we developed a speedrun routing benchmark that can be used to compare the performance of different optimization methods, and we conducted an extensive evaluation of these techniques using a variety of speedrun routing instances.  Our results show that meta-learning methods, specifically those that use evolutionary algorithms, are particularly well-suited to solving speedrun routing problems efficiently.  However, we also found that the performance of these meta-learning methods can be significantly improved by incorporating additional search strategies, such as simulated annealing, and by using a more diverse population of solutions.  Our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the speedrun routing problem and its relationship to meta-learning methods, and it offers a number of insights that can inform the design of more efficient speedrun routing algorithms.  Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our findings in the context of speedrunning and optimization research.  The code and data used in this study are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/stephenlightfoot/speedrun-optimization. that maximizes reward expectations. However, FRL's performance is often compromised 
by communication latency and the need for a centralized server.

challenges by utilizing local policy learning, decentralized gradient 
optimization, and peer-to-peer communication. Experimental results show that 
FedRLP significantly outperforms existing FRL methods, achieving a 20% 
improvement in average reward and surpassing the performance of centralized RL.

outages. The proposed method is expected to facilitate the practical application 
of RL in real-world settings, where data privacy and communication reliability are

The active inference framework offers a distinct perspective on reward-based decision-making, diverging from traditional reinforcement learning approaches. In this research, we introduce a novel method for defining reward structures within active inference. We demonstrate that the standard reward function can be redefined as the outcome of a probabilistic inference process, in which a reward network generates a probability distribution over possible rewards given an input state and action. We propose a simple, feed-forward reward network that replicates the behavior of the conventional active inference model, while also investigating the implications of using a more complex, recurrent reward network on model performance and computational efficiency. We assess the impact of reward network design on inference time, decision-making, and the ability to learn from sparse rewards, revealing that the proposed reward networks can learn effectively from sparse data and outperform the standard active inference model in certain scenarios. Additionally, we examine the potential benefits of employing a more complex reward network, suggesting that it may offer advantages in specific contexts. The active inference framework's unique perspective on reward learning, combined with the proposed reward networks, provides a promising approach for tackling complex reward-based learning problems. understanding of mappings between metric spaces. In this paper, we introduce a
novel fixed point outcome for a class of mappings that meet specific
self-mapping criteria within a metric space of the form $(S,d)$. Our work

Mappings that encompass both continuous and non-continuous elements. The
research presented here is grounded in the fixed point theorems of Reiter and

illustrative examples. The utility of our research is further demonstrated
through the derivation of new fixed point theorems for mappings within

The evaluation of state-of-the-art Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) systems is often based on accuracy scores derived from datasets of annotated incorrect sentences. However, this approach has a significant flaw: rare errors, which make up a small portion of the data, receive excessive weight in the evaluation process. As a result, GEC systems that excel at correcting common errors but struggle with rare ones may be unfairly ranked behind systems that excel at correcting rare errors but underperform on common ones. To address this issue, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called the Weighted Error Rate (WER). By reassigning weights to errors based on their frequency, WER provides a more balanced assessment of GEC systems' performance. Furthermore, WER can be easily adapted to assess other language tasks beyond GEC. To demonstrate the effectiveness of WER, we conducted a thorough evaluation of cutting-edge GEC systems, which revealed that WER yields a more nuanced ranking of the systems than traditional accuracy scores. Additionally, WER enabled us to identify areas where GEC systems require further improvement. The Weighted Error Rate metric is available for public use under an open-source license. The evaluation code and results can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/ritchielyn/WeightedErrorRate. The evaluation dataset used in this study is also available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ucl-nlp/GECC. The research was supported by the UK Research and Innovation's CDT programme. This paper introduces AppealNet, a novel approach that dynamically adjusts model complexity to balance accuracy and computational expense in deep learning models. By utilizing a single network with adjustable parameters, AppealNet optimizes the network's depth and width, and instead of employing pruning or compression, it selectively modifies a subset of parameters. AppealNet then determines the optimal configuration through a reinforcement learning strategy, guided by a policy network trained on a small dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that AppealNet achieves comparable accuracy to the full model, while significantly reducing computation cost, outperforming existing pruning and compression methods. AppealNet also offers real-time adaptability, enabling it to adjust its accuracy and computation in response to changing input conditions. AppealNet's source code is publicly available on GitHub. We introduce a novel point geometry image, called the point geometry image (PGI), to convert 3D point clouds into 2D images that retain spatial information by encoding depth and inter-point distances. PGI serves as a universal image representation of a 3D point cloud, which can be applied to various tasks. Leveraging PGI, we propose a two-stage learning approach for 3D point cloud segmentation, incorporating a point classification stage and a refinement stage. The first stage utilizes a 2D neural network to extract features from PGI, while the second stage refines the point labels using a graph convolution network. Experimental results demonstrate that PGI outperforms traditional methods in encoding 3D point clouds, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the S3DIS dataset. We investigate how to integrate fairness considerations into the training process to cater to clients with distinct objectives. Our analysis reveals that these fairness-aware methods can adapt to clients with unique objectives, leading to optimal results. Furthermore, we observe that these approaches can be adapted to address fairness concerns in other domains, such as text classification. Our research marks a significant step towards creating more robust and client-centric federated learning systems. This research explores the development of a speech recognition system for the Basque language without access to the audio data of its target language. Instead, our method leverages the audio data of a related language, namely Spanish, and adapts it to Basque by utilizing a bilingual text set. The proposed approach involves two key innovations: first, a technique for generating phoneme alignments in the target language without access to the audio; second, a novel method for aligning the alignments of source and target languages based on text data. Our findings indicate that this approach yields promising results, with a significant improvement over a baseline system, achieving a substantial 34.83% reduction in word error rate. Furthermore, our method demonstrates its ability to adapt across different languages, achieving comparable improvements in other language pairs, such as Welsh-English and Scottish Gaelic English. The presented work is a pioneering achievement in developing a speech recognition system for the Basque language without access to the audio data of its target language. Furthermore, we have developed a method to identify voters with significant influence within complex networks and tested it on real-world data from the 2014 European Parliament elections. Our findings demonstrate that the political landscape in Europe is characterized by a diverse range of opinion distributions, with some countries experiencing a polarized climate, while others feature a more fragmented and scattered landscape. Notably, the most influential voters are typically found in urban areas, particularly in countries like Germany and the UK. These results have the potential to inform parties on how best to allocate their resources to maximize their electoral prospects. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights for politicians seeking to effectively engage with their constituents and adapt their messaging to resonate with different audience segments. The quality of images captured in dynamic scenes is often compromised due to motion blur, resulting in blurry images that are difficult to restore accurately. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the potential of image restoration to improve the quality of images captured in these environments. By predicting the image restoration potential (IRP) - a measure of an image's quality and suitability for restoration - we can identify and prioritize images that are most in need of improvement. This allows us to select the best possible image from a sequence, either by restoring the image in real-time or by selecting it as the input for image processing applications. To achieve this, we have developed a deep convolutional neural network that can accurately predict the IRP of images based on their content and visual characteristics. This approach has been successfully demonstrated in a variety of applications, including real-time image enhancement, image restoration, and object detection. The results show that our approach can significantly improve the quality of images captured in dynamic scenes, resulting in enhanced visual experiences and improved performance in various computer vision tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explore the use of IRP prediction for image restoration and its applications in computer vision. This paper explores the mathematical underpinnings of databases and queries, 
reexamining how limits and colimits are defined in database relations. 
The discussion delves into applying concepts like adjoint functors, 
composition of relations, and free monads to achieve this understanding. 
The study also touches on how databases can be represented as categories 
and how queries can be viewed as a subset of functor transformations. 
The paper concludes by investigating the relationship between data and computation, 
specifically through the lens of topos theory and its implications for databases. 
This work draws upon and synthesizes existing research from multiple fields, 
including database theory, category theory, type systems, and topos theory. 
These diverse sources are integrated to provide a cohesive understanding of 
database relations rooted in category theory. 
Keywords: database relations, category theory, limits, colimits, adjoint functors, 
composition of relations, topos theory, database semantics.

expressed as $\CAN(v, t, k, n) \leq v^n \cdot 2^{1-k/n}$ for fixed values of $v$ and $t$. 
This limit is most relevant when the Covering Array Number is large, 
and the derived bound is consistent with existing bounds for small values of $n$. 
The new bound is also similar in form to a previously established limit on the Size of Covering Set (SOS) in a related but distinct context, 
where the derived bound is expressed as $SOS(v, t, k, n) \leq v^n \cdot 2^{1-k/n}$.

We introduce the Multiverse, a novel approach to trajectory forecasting that
generates multiple accurate predictions for a single future time point.
Diverging from traditional methods, which produce a single predicted path,
our model generates a set of possible routes, each representing a plausible
outcome. By treating future movement trajectories as the result of uncertain
events, we employ a sampling-based approach to simulate various possible
scenarios and calculate the likelihood of each resulting path.
To demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, we conducted experiments using
the Oxford Robot Car dataset, which revealed that the Multiverse outperformed
existing trajectory forecasting techniques in terms of accuracy and coverage.
The resulting predictions provide valuable insights into potential future
scenarios, enabling more informed decision-making. The code implementing the
Multiverse is openly available on GitHub. The associated data and results can
be found on the project's website. Furthermore, we have developed a web-based
visualisation tool to facilitate the exploration of predicted trajectories.

The creation of detailed driving environments is a critical component in the development of self-driving vehicles. Current methods for generating these settings rely on a combination of user input and random simulation, but this approach often results in environments that are unrealistic and time-consuming to design. Our approach involves defining a structured representation of driving scenes using a set of symbolic rules, which are then used to create a directed graph that represents the environment. By applying these rules in a structured manner, we are able to produce a wide variety of driving environments that are both realistic and efficient to design. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we have created a dataset of 100,000 driving environments and conducted a thorough evaluation of their diversity and quality. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods for driving environment generation, and we believe that this method has the potential to significantly accelerate the development of self-driving vehicles. Gumbel-based algorithms have been widely used in machine learning literature for tasks such as top-k selection, categorical sampling, and categorical reparameterization. However, the existing literature lacks a comprehensive proof of their theoretical reliability. This study fills this gap by providing a rigorous theoretical foundation for Gumbel algorithms, demonstrating their reliability in sampling and reparameterization. Our proof relies on the Gumbel-max and Gumbel-sort inequalities, which establish the statistical reliability of Gumbel algorithms. This work also provides a novel explanation of the efficacy of Gumbel algorithms, grounded in the concept of maximum entropy. Additionally, we adapt our theoretical findings to the context of Dirichlet distributions and derive a new concentration inequality for discrete random variables. Our study also explores the application of Gumbel-based algorithms to the task of top-k selection, providing a theoretical understanding of their performance. Finally, we conduct an empirical evaluation of the top-k selection algorithm on various datasets, which aligns with our theoretical predictions. Our proof is accompanied by accompanying code available at https://github.com/ashish-kr/gumbel-reliability. The research proposes a hypothesis that, when working with common data, self-supervised learning tends to focus on common characteristics, which often results in class imbalance. To address this issue, a new method called the Class Balanced Self-supervised Learning (CSSL) framework is developed. The CSSS framework is comprised of two primary components: the Class Imbalance Augmentation (CIA) module, which generates balanced samples from the original data, and the Balanced Contrastive Loss (BCL) module, which calculates the loss for the balanced samples. The CIA module employs a novel method to create balanced samples by combining the original data with its shifted versions. The BCL module then computes the loss for these balanced samples. The performance of the proposed CSSS framework is evaluated on various datasets, including ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and the Digits7 and Digits62 datasets, and is compared to existing self-supervised learning methods. A novel approach called TNT (Tomography Network Traceroute) is designed to
determine the path of MPLS tunnels in live networks. By sending packets with
specific TTL values and observing where they are dropped, TNT can identify
MPLS tunnels. Building on previous work, the standard Traceroute tool, TNT uses
a more advanced method that detects MPLS tunnels even when they are not
explicitly marked. In our evaluation, we demonstrate that TNT successfully
identifies the complete sequence of tunnels in a multi-hop path and can even
detect tunnels that extend beyond a single hop. Furthermore, the results show
that the additional information provided by TNT enables more accurate
determination of network topology. In our experiments, the average error rate
was significantly reduced, with improvements of up to 90% compared to a
baseline method. Additionally, the results indicate that the additional
information provided by TNT can improve the accuracy of network topology
inference, with average reductions in error rates of up to 50%. Overall, the
findings highlight the effectiveness of TNT in improving network tomography. The
source code for TNT is publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/USC-CKD/TNT.

The increasing use of machine learning models in high-stakes applications has led to a growing demand for explanations about their predictions. Although numerous attribution-based methods have been developed to meet this need, they often provide explanations that are specific to individual predictions. However, these explanations can be unreliable when subjected to minor changes in the input data, potentially resulting in misleading information. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a Bayesian framework to quantify the uncertainty associated with attribution-based explanations. Our method involves calculating the expected value of an attribution score by averaging over all possible input data given the uncertainty model, which is then used to generate stable explanations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting a comprehensive evaluation of its performance in comparison to existing methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results show that our method produces more consistent explanations than other techniques, even when the input data is slightly altered. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can be integrated with existing explanation methods to enhance their robustness. Our findings highlight the importance of considering uncertainty in the generation of explanations and provide a practical method for improving their reliability. This metric is then used in conjunction with a planning algorithm that leverages a model predictive control framework to produce stable and efficient paths in real-time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating stable and efficient paths for manipulation tasks. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first attempt to integrate control-theoretic techniques into real-time planning frameworks. This paper introduces Gemino, a novel video compression system that leverages
the inherent structure of videos to enhance encoding efficiency at low bitrates.
Building upon the previous Gemini system, Gemino further optimizes video quality
by incorporating a more sophisticated motion model and refined loop structure.
The key innovations of Gemino lie in its motion model, which utilizes a combination
of optical flow and sparse motion vectors to capture detailed motion patterns,
and its loop structure design, which identifies and encodes motion vectors in a
more efficient manner. The results demonstrate that Gemino achieves a 10.5%
improvement in PSNR and 15.1% increase in SSIM compared to traditional codecs,
while outperforming the current state-of-the-art Gemini system by 0.5% in PSNR and
2.0% in SSIM. The accompanying code and model will be publicly available at

Moreover, our S2 method can be easily integrated with existing weak supervision techniques, resulting in improved performance on various benchmarks. We investigate the impact of delayed optical feedback on the behavior of microlasers, specifically their single-photon excursions, in terms of their distribution and how they vary. Our research focuses on microlasers that produce random pulses, and we discover that delayed optical feedback significantly alters the likelihood of these pulses. Furthermore, we find that the probability of these pulses changes in a unique way, depending on the strength of the feedback, and that this behavior is consistent with previous findings on the stability of optical systems. Additionally, we explore the characteristics of the highest and lowest energy pulses experienced by the microlaser.
